title: When Sally Brings a Chinese AGI to Class in September
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard uses the release of Kimi K3—a 2.8 trillion parameter open-weight model from Chinese lab Moonshot AI—as a lens for examining what it means for education when AGI-level capability becomes freely available to every student. Unlike previous AI milestones, an open-weight model that anyone can run locally represents a genuinely new threat to the traditional assumptions of schooling: it cannot be blocked, filtered, or fee-gated. Bauschard describes AGI as fundamentally changing the oldest constraint in business and education—talent scarcity—making cognitive labor elastically scalable for any institution or individual with compute access. The recursive self-improvement dynamics of advanced AI systems suggest the pace of this shift is motorized, not gradual. For education, the crisis is not chatbot misuse but something deeper: if AGI represents a "peak of every field, infinitely copyable, swarming, compounding workforce," then what exactly is education for? The piece argues that the scenario nobody planned for has arrived: a trillion-dollar capability handed to everyone simultaneously, for free.
points: Open-weight models like Kimi K3 represent a qualitatively different threat to schools than API-gated AI: they cannot be blocked, filtered, or fee-gated by institutions
AGI makes cognitive labor elastically scalable—any individual or institution can field an arbitrarily large expert workforce for the price of compute, erasing expertise as a competitive moat
Education faces a foundational question: if a freely available AI can perform at the peak of every field, what exactly are schools preparing students to become?
quotes: On July 16, a Chinese lab called Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 — 2.8 trillion parameters, the largest open-weight model ever built.

In blind head-to-head testing, developers preferred it to some leading American system for frontend code, and on the aggregate intelligence index it sits inside the frontier tier, behind only the top two closed U.S.

Some at the frontierare saying more than that: that K3 fulfills two of the remaining ingredients of AGI — initial signs of recursive self-improvement and the ability to learn on its own — making it, in their telling, “AGI-ish.” [As I noted here, we are also starting to see evidence of this in Sol] On July 27, the weights go public.
Read that second sentence again, because it is the one that matters for education.

In one week, anyone on Earth — any student, any school, any ministry of education, any teenager with a gaming rig — will be able to download something at or near the frontier of machine intelligence andrun it themselves.
I’m not the one who settles that Serious people are making the case that K3 is early-stage AGI.

On this week’s Moonshots emergency pod, Dave Blundin argued that the recursive self-improvement threshold has already been crossed — that a system doesn’t need Einstein-level genius to bootstrap itself (a point previously made by Yoshua Bengio), it only needs to improve its own kernel for a tenfold speedup, and, as explained, Moonshot’s release materials describe K3 designing chips and writing kernels for its own successor.
Other serious people will call this benchmark theater and label inflation, and they may be right.
